claim: Lifespan is shortened by mating in C. elegans hermaphrodites.
source: Lifespan is shortened by mating, but these deleterious effects must be delayed long enough for successful reproduction.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Susceptibility to brief mating-induced death is caused by the loss of protection upon self-sperm depletion.
source: Susceptibility to brief mating-induced death is caused by the loss of protection upon self-sperm depletion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing young hermaphrodites with self-sperm are protected while old hermaphrodites without self-sperm are susceptible.

claim: Self-sperm maintains the expression of a DAF-2 insulin-like antagonist, INS-37.
source: Self-sperm maintains the expression of a DAF-2 insulin-like antagonist, INS-37, which promotes the nuclear localization of intestinal HLH-30/TFEB, a key pro-longevity regulator.
evidence: Supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data showing ins-37 is upregulated in wild-type compared to fog-2 hermaphrodites.

claim: INS-37 promotes the nuclear localization of intestinal HLH-30/TFEB.
source: Self-sperm maintains the expression of a DAF-2 insulin-like antagonist, INS-37, which promotes the nuclear localization of intestinal HLH-30/TFEB, a key pro-longevity regulator.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of ins-37 reduces nuclear HLH-30::GFP.

claim: Mating induces the agonist INS-8.
source: Mating induces the agonist INS-8, promoting HLH-30 nuclear exit and subsequent death.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis and ins-8p::gfp reporter data showing increased ins-8 expression after mating.

claim: INS-8 promotes HLH-30 nuclear exit and subsequent death.
source: Mating induces the agonist INS-8, promoting HLH-30 nuclear exit and subsequent death.
evidence: Supported by data showing knockdown of ins-8 prevents HLH-30 cytoplasmic localization and protects from mating-induced death.

claim: HLH-30/TFEB plays a protective role against mating-induced death.
source: In opposition to the protective role of HLH-30 and DAF-16/FOXO, TOR/LET-363 and the IIS-regulated Zn-finger transcription factor PQM-1 promote seminal-fluid-induced killing.
evidence: Supported by data showing hlh-30 mutants are susceptible to brief mating and HLH-30::GFP overexpression provides protection.

claim: DAF-16/FOXO plays a protective role against mating-induced death.
source: In opposition to the protective role of HLH-30 and DAF-16/FOXO, TOR/LET-363 and the IIS-regulated Zn-finger transcription factor PQM-1 promote seminal-fluid-induced killing.
evidence: Supported by data showing daf-16 mutants are susceptible to brief mating even when young.

claim: TOR/LET-363 promotes seminal-fluid-induced killing.
source: In opposition to the protective role of HLH-30 and DAF-16/FOXO, TOR/LET-363 and the IIS-regulated Zn-finger transcription factor PQM-1 promote seminal-fluid-induced killing.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduction of let-363 prevents brief mating-induced death in fog-2 females.

claim: PQM-1 promotes seminal-fluid-induced killing.
source: In opposition to the protective role of HLH-30 and DAF-16/FOXO, TOR/LET-363 and the IIS-regulated Zn-finger transcription factor PQM-1 promote seminal-fluid-induced killing.
evidence: Supported by data showing pqm-1 mutants are resistant to both brief and long-term mating.

claim: Males compete with one another to pass on their own genomes, often at the expense of female health.
source: The battle between the sexes is played out across the animal kingdom: males compete with one another to pass on their own genomes, often at the expense of female health, and females, in turn, must devise strategies to reduce the deleterious effects of mating in order to successfully complete reproduction.
evidence: This is a general statement about sexual antagonism supported by established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: Signals from males kill hermaphrodites through germline activation.
source: Sexual antagonism is evident in Caenorhabditis elegans, where signals from males kill hermaphrodites through three distinct mechanisms: germline activation (Shi and Murphy, 2014), seminal fluid transfer (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and, at high doses, male pheromone toxicity (Maures et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Signals from males kill hermaphrodites through seminal fluid transfer.
source: Sexual antagonism is evident in Caenorhabditis elegans, where signals from males kill hermaphrodites through three distinct mechanisms: germline activation (Shi and Murphy, 2014), seminal fluid transfer (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and, at high doses, male pheromone toxicity (Maures et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Signals from males kill hermaphrodites through male pheromone toxicity at high doses.
source: Sexual antagonism is evident in Caenorhabditis elegans, where signals from males kill hermaphrodites through three distinct mechanisms: germline activation (Shi and Murphy, 2014), seminal fluid transfer (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and, at high doses, male pheromone toxicity (Maures et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: C. elegans are hermaphrodites and do not require males to reproduce.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans are hermaphrodites and thus do not require males to reproduce; in fact, males are normally rare in nature (~1/1000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans biology.

claim: Males are normally rare in nature (~1/1000) in C. elegans populations.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans are hermaphrodites and thus do not require males to reproduce; in fact, males are normally rare in nature (~1/1000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans populations.

claim: Brief bursts of mating with males can be beneficial for the species due to increased outcrossing.
source: Brief bursts of mating with males can be beneficial for the species due to increased outcrossing (Kimble, 1988), but males are quickly eliminated by dispersal (Wegewitz et al., 2008; Anderson et al., 2010) and by their own pheromones (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Males are quickly eliminated by dispersal.
source: Brief bursts of mating with males can be beneficial for the species due to increased outcrossing (Kimble, 1988), but males are quickly eliminated by dispersal (Wegewitz et al., 2008; Anderson et al., 2010) and by their own pheromones (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Males are quickly eliminated by their own pheromones.
source: Brief bursts of mating with males can be beneficial for the species due to increased outcrossing (Kimble, 1988), but males are quickly eliminated by dispersal (Wegewitz et al., 2008; Anderson et al., 2010) and by their own pheromones (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Seminal fluid transfer induces death of mothers just after they have produced all of that male's progeny.
source: While germline activation is necessary for reproduction and the resulting lifespan decrease is shared both across sexes and species, seminal fluid (SF) killing appears to be used specifically for the purpose of 'sperm competition' (that is, competition between males) within the species: seminal fluid transfer induces death of mothers just after they have produced all of that male's progeny, eliminating the possibility of the mother re-mating with a different male (Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Seminal fluid killing eliminates the possibility of the mother re-mating with a different male.
source: While germline activation is necessary for reproduction and the resulting lifespan decrease is shared both across sexes and species, seminal fluid (SF) killing appears to be used specifically for the purpose of 'sperm competition' (that is, competition between males) within the species: seminal fluid transfer induces death of mothers just after they have produced all of that male's progeny, eliminating the possibility of the mother re-mating with a different male (Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of death and the concept of sperm competition.

claim: Mating-induced death occurs only after C. elegans hermaphrodites produce all their progeny.
source: We noted previously that mating-induced death occurs only after C. elegans hermaphrodites produce all their progeny (Shi and Murphy, 2014); this delay is necessary for successful reproduction, but the underlying mechanism allowing this balance was previously unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Self-sperm are protective against short-term mating-induced death specifically in hermaphroditic mothers.
source: In an accompanying manuscript, Booth et al. report that self-sperm are protective against short-term mating-induced death specifically in hermaphroditic mothers (Booth et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to accompanying manuscript.

claim: Young hermaphrodites that mate during a brief interaction with males are protected from mating-induced death.
source: Unlike older hermaphrodites, young hermaphrodites that mate during a brief interaction with males are protected from this mating-induced death (Booth et al., 2019; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by citation and Figure 1A,B showing survival curves.

claim: Young feminized (fog-2(q71), fem-1(hc17)) worms lacking self-sperm exhibit significant acceleration of death after brief mating with males.
source: By contrast, young feminized (i.e. lacking self-sperm; fog-2(q71), fem-1(hc17)) worms exhibit significant acceleration of death after brief mating with males (Booth et al., 2019; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that self-sperm are protective.
evidence: Supported by citation and Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing survival curves.

claim: Wild-type N2 hermaphrodites have reduced lifespan after 2 hr mating on day 7 of adulthood.
source: Day 7 N2 unmated: 13.8 ± 0.5 days; mated: 10.0 ± 0.4 days, p<0.0001.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data with statistical significance.

claim: Wild-type N2 hermaphrodites have normal lifespan when brief mating occurs on day 3.
source: Day 3 N2 unmated: 14.1 ± 0.7 days; mated: 13.9 ± 0.6 days, p=0.8481
evidence: Supported by lifespan data showing no significant difference.

claim: Self-spermless fog-2(q71) are susceptible to 2 hr mating on both day 3 and day 7 of adulthood.
source: Day three fog-2 unmated: 19.7 ± 0.7 days; mated: 15.4 ± 0.7 days, p<0.0001; Day seven fog-2 unmated: 21.0 ± 0.6 days; mated: 14.8 ± 0.5 days, p<0.0001.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data with statistical significance.

claim: Mating with fog-2 males (which are functionally wild type) leads to lifespan decrease in fog-2 self-spermless hermaphrodites.
source: Day 3 fog-2 unmated: 18.2 ± 0.8 days; mated with fog-2 males: 12.6 ± 0.7 days, p<0.0001
evidence: Supported by lifespan data with statistical significance.

claim: Both sperm-containing and spermless males induce death in young and old fog-2 mothers at equal rates.
source: To determine whether brief mating acts through the male sperm/germline pathway or through the seminal fluid pathway, we mated fer-6 males, which are spermless but still contain seminal fluid (Figure 1D,E; Argon and Ward, 1980; Gems and Riddle, 1996), or fog-2 males, which contain male sperm and thus essentially are like wild type (Schedl and Kimble, 1988), with fog-2 (self-spermless) females; both sperm-containing and spermless males induce death in young and old fog-2 mothers at equal rates, suggesting that the death-inducing factor is not sperm.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 1D,E and citations.

claim: The death-inducing factor in brief mating is not male sperm.
source: both sperm-containing and spermless males induce death in young and old fog-2 mothers at equal rates, suggesting that the death-inducing factor is not sperm.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing equal effects of sperm-containing and spermless males.

claim: Brief mating-induced death acts through the seminal fluid pathway.
source: The dispensability of male sperm suggests that brief mating-induced death acts through the seminal fluid pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing male sperm is not required for the effect.

claim: daf-22 males induce the same brief mating lifespan effect as wild-type males.
source: However, daf-22 males induce the same brief mating lifespan effect as wild-type males.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 1F-I.

claim: 2 hr treatment on high-dose male pheromone-conditioned plates does not shorten the lifespan of either wild-type or fog-2 females.
source: Similarly, 2 hr treatment on high-dose male pheromone-conditioned plates ('MCP'; plates pre-treated with 30 males, then removed prior to experiment) does not shorten the lifespan of either wild-type or fog-2 females (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Self-sperm protects against brief mating-induced death in a manner that is independent of both male sperm and pheromone effects.
source: Together, these data suggest that self-sperm protects against brief mating-induced death in a manner that is independent of both male sperm and pheromone effects, and acts through the seminal fluid/IIS pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing male sperm and pheromones are not required.

claim: Insulin-IGF-1 signaling (IIS) mediates seminal fluid-induced killing by inducing DAF-16/FOXO nuclear exit.
source: We previously showed that Insulin-IGF-1 signaling (IIS) mediates seminal fluid-induced killing by inducing DAF-16/FOXO nuclear exit (Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: daf-16 mutants are susceptible to brief mating, even when young.
source: We find that daf-16 mutants are also susceptible to brief mating, even when young (Figure 2A), suggesting that DAF-16 activity is critical for resistance to brief mating.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 2A.

claim: DAF-16 activity is critical for resistance to brief mating.
source: We find that daf-16 mutants are also susceptible to brief mating, even when young (Figure 2A), suggesting that DAF-16 activity is critical for resistance to brief mating.
evidence: This is an inference from the daf-16 mutant phenotype.

claim: Long-lived daf-2/Insulin receptor mutants are better protected than wild-type worms on Day 8 of adulthood.
source: Long-lived daf-2/Insulin receptor mutants, although susceptible to long-term mating, are better protected than wild-type worms on Day 8 of adulthood (Figure 2B), exhibiting the opposite phenotype as daf-16 mutants.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 2B.

claim: DAF-16::GFP in fog-2 (self-spermless) mutants moves out of the nucleus upon brief mating.
source: Furthermore, DAF-16::GFP in fog-2 (self-spermless) mutants moves out of the nucleus upon brief mating (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 2C-D.

claim: ins-37 is strikingly upregulated in wild-type compared to fog-2 L4 hermaphrodites.
source: However, of the remaining differences, the conserved insulin-like peptide ins-37 is strikingly upregulated in wild-type compared to fog-2 L4 hermaphrodites (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that this germline-expressed (Ebbing et al., 2018) signaling molecule is only highly expressed when self-sperm are present.
evidence: Supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: ins-37 is a germline-expressed signaling molecule.
source: However, of the remaining differences, the conserved insulin-like peptide ins-37 is strikingly upregulated in wild-type compared to fog-2 L4 hermaphrodites (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that this germline-expressed (Ebbing et al., 2018) signaling molecule is only highly expressed when self-sperm are present.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ins-37 is only highly expressed when self-sperm are present.
source: However, of the remaining differences, the conserved insulin-like peptide ins-37 is strikingly upregulated in wild-type compared to fog-2 L4 hermaphrodites (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that this germline-expressed (Ebbing et al., 2018) signaling molecule is only highly expressed when self-sperm are present.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of wild-type and fog-2 expression data.

claim: RNAi of ins-37 in wild-type (N2) worms shortens their lifespan after brief mating.
source: Indeed, RNAi of ins-37 in wild-type (N2) worms shortens their lifespan after brief mating (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), despite the presence of self-sperm, suggesting that ins-37 is key for self-sperm-mediated protection from mating.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 3C.

claim: ins-37 is key for self-sperm-mediated protection from mating.
source: Indeed, RNAi of ins-37 in wild-type (N2) worms shortens their lifespan after brief mating (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), despite the presence of self-sperm, suggesting that ins-37 is key for self-sperm-mediated protection from mating.
evidence: This is an inference from the ins-37 RNAi phenotype.

claim: INS-37 acts as a DAF-2 antagonist during development.
source: INS-37 may act as a self-sperm-induced antagonist of the insulin receptor, DAF-2, consistent with a recent report that INS-37 acts a DAF-2 antagonist during development (Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: INS-37 may act as a self-sperm-induced antagonist of the insulin receptor, DAF-2.
source: INS-37 may act as a self-sperm-induced antagonist of the insulin receptor, DAF-2, consistent with a recent report that INS-37 acts a DAF-2 antagonist during development (Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and previous reports.

claim: Spermless females differ in genes whose promoters contain the predicted binding motif for the HLH-30/TFEB transcription factor.
source: Our transcriptional data revealed that spermless females differ not only in expression of sperm proteins and ins-37 but also in genes whose promoters contain the predicted binding motif for the HLH-30/TFEB transcription factor (Reimand et al., 2007; Grove et al., 2009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which has been previously implicated in longevity regulation through its control of lipid metabolism and lysosomal autophagy.
evidence: Supported by transcriptional data and motif analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: HLH-30/TFEB has been previously implicated in longevity regulation through its control of lipid metabolism and lysosomal autophagy.
source: Our transcriptional data revealed that spermless females differ not only in expression of sperm proteins and ins-37 but also in genes whose promoters contain the predicted binding motif for the HLH-30/TFEB transcription factor (Reimand et al., 2007; Grove et al., 2009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which has been previously implicated in longevity regulation through its control of lipid metabolism and lysosomal autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLH-30/TFEB function.

claim: Mutants that produce an excess of self-sperm (fem-3(q20)) are protected from brief mating-induced death for a longer period of their lifespan than wild-type hermaphrodites.
source: Mutants that produce an excess of self-sperm (fem-3(q20)) (Rosenquist and Kimble, 1988) are protected from brief mating-induced death for a longer period of their lifespan than wild-type hermaphrodites (Booth et al., 2019), and we found that the HLH-30 binding motif is also enriched in promoters of genes that are up-regulated in (fem-3(q20)) hermaphrodites compared to animals with normal levels of sperm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by citation and transcriptional data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The HLH-30 binding motif is enriched in promoters of genes that are up-regulated in fem-3(q20) hermaphrodites compared to animals with normal levels of sperm.
source: Mutants that produce an excess of self-sperm (fem-3(q20)) (Rosenquist and Kimble, 1988) are protected from brief mating-induced death for a longer period of their lifespan than wild-type hermaphrodites (Booth et al., 2019), and we found that the HLH-30 binding motif is also enriched in promoters of genes that are up-regulated in (fem-3(q20)) hermaphrodites compared to animals with normal levels of sperm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by transcriptional data and motif analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TFEB/HLH-30 acts downstream of the TOR pathway.
source: TFEB/HLH-30 acts downstream of several longevity pathways, notably the TOR pathway (Lapierre et al., 2013; Nakamura et al., 2016), and DAF-16 and HLH-30 were also recently shown to cooperate under many conditions (Lin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DAF-16 and HLH-30 cooperate under many conditions.
source: TFEB/HLH-30 acts downstream of several longevity pathways, notably the TOR pathway (Lapierre et al., 2013; Nakamura et al., 2016), and DAF-16 and HLH-30 were also recently shown to cooperate under many conditions (Lin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: hlh-30 mutants are susceptible to brief mating even when young.
source: To determine whether HLH-30 is required for self-sperm protection, we briefly mated hlh-30 mutants on Day 3 of adulthood; similar to loss of ins-37 and daf-16, hlh-30 mutants are susceptible to brief mating even when young, suggesting that self-sperm protection requires HLH-30 activity (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 4A.

claim: Self-sperm protection requires HLH-30 activity.
source: To determine whether HLH-30 is required for self-sperm protection, we briefly mated hlh-30 mutants on Day 3 of adulthood; similar to loss of ins-37 and daf-16, hlh-30 mutants are susceptible to brief mating even when young, suggesting that self-sperm protection requires HLH-30 activity (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is an inference from the hlh-30 mutant phenotype.

claim: HLH-30::GFP is nuclearly localized in the intestine of young animals that have self-sperm.
source: We found that HLH-30::GFP is nuclearly localized in the intestine of young animals that have self-sperm, becoming diffuse with age as self-sperm is depleted (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: HLH-30::GFP becomes diffuse with age as self-sperm is depleted.
source: We found that HLH-30::GFP is nuclearly localized in the intestine of young animals that have self-sperm, becoming diffuse with age as self-sperm is depleted (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Fewer self-spermless animals display nuclearly localized HLH-30::GFP.
source: Fewer self-spermless animals display nuclearly localized HLH-30::GFP, while more animals with excess self-sperm exhibit nuclearly localized HLH-30::GFP (Figure 4E–F; note scale).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4E-F.

claim: More animals with excess self-sperm exhibit nuclearly localized HLH-30::GFP.
source: Fewer self-spermless animals display nuclearly localized HLH-30::GFP, while more animals with excess self-sperm exhibit nuclearly localized HLH-30::GFP (Figure 4E–F; note scale).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Loss of ins-37 reduces nuclear HLH-30::GFP.
source: Moreover, loss of ins-37 reduces nuclear HLH-30::GFP (Figure 4G–I), suggesting that INS-37 acts upstream of HLH-30.
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4G-I.

claim: INS-37 acts upstream of HLH-30.
source: Moreover, loss of ins-37 reduces nuclear HLH-30::GFP (Figure 4G–I), suggesting that INS-37 acts upstream of HLH-30.
evidence: This is an inference from the effect of ins-37 loss on HLH-30 localization.

claim: The HLH-30::GFP strain overexpresses functional HLH-30 protein.
source: The HLH-30::GFP strain overexpresses functional HLH-30 protein, so we wondered whether these animals are better protected from brief mating-induced death; indeed, no lifespan reduction was observed in the HLH-30::GFP strain after mating for 12 hr, a length of mating that shortens WT lifespan (Figure 4J–K), suggesting that the additional HLH-30 provides a protective effect.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 4J-K.

claim: No lifespan reduction was observed in the HLH-30::GFP strain after mating for 12 hr.
source: The HLH-30::GFP strain overexpresses functional HLH-30 protein, so we wondered whether these animals are better protected from brief mating-induced death; indeed, no lifespan reduction was observed in the HLH-30::GFP strain after mating for 12 hr, a length of mating that shortens WT lifespan (Figure 4J–K), suggesting that the additional HLH-30 provides a protective effect.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 4J-K.

claim: Additional HLH-30 provides a protective effect against mating-induced death.
source: The HLH-30::GFP strain overexpresses functional HLH-30 protein, so we wondered whether these animals are better protected from brief mating-induced death; indeed, no lifespan reduction was observed in the HLH-30::GFP strain after mating for 12 hr, a length of mating that shortens WT lifespan (Figure 4J–K), suggesting that the additional HLH-30 provides a protective effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the HLH-30::GFP overexpression phenotype.

claim: Longer mating reduces both nuclear HLH-30::GFP localization and lifespan.
source: However, longer mating reduces both nuclear HLH-30::GFP localization and lifespan (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–K), suggesting that prolonged mating can eventually overwhelm the protection conferred by HLH-30.
evidence: Supported by imaging and lifespan data in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-K.

claim: Prolonged mating can eventually overwhelm the protection conferred by HLH-30.
source: However, longer mating reduces both nuclear HLH-30::GFP localization and lifespan (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–K), suggesting that prolonged mating can eventually overwhelm the protection conferred by HLH-30.
evidence: This is an inference from the effects of prolonged mating on HLH-30 localization and lifespan.

claim: TOR signaling has been implicated in longevity regulation from yeast through humans, including C. elegans.
source: TOR signaling has been implicated in longevity regulation from yeast through humans, including C. elegans (Kapahi and Hansen, 2010; Kaeberlein and Shamieh, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TOR negatively regulates TFEB/HLH-30's nuclear localization and activity.
source: TOR negatively regulates TFEB/HLH-30's nuclear localization and activity (Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Most positive regulators of TOR signaling were modestly downregulated in conditions in which worms are protected from brief mating.
source: Through genome-wide transcriptional comparisons, we observed that most positive regulators of TOR signaling were modestly downregulated in conditions in which worms are protected from brief mating (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by transcriptional data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Reduction of the worm TOR homolog, let-363, prevented the lifespan decrease caused by brief mating in young spermless (fog-2) females.
source: Indeed, we found that reduction of the worm TOR homolog, let-363, prevented the lifespan decrease caused by brief mating in young spermless (fog-2) females (Figure 5C–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 5C-D.

claim: RNAi reduction of rict-1, daf-15, and raga-1 prevented brief mating-induced death in Day 3 fog-2 females.
source: Similarly, RNAi reduction of other TOR pathway components, including rict-1, daf-15, and raga-1, also prevented brief mating-induced death in Day 3 fog-2 females, and Day 7 (sperm-exhausted) raga-1 mutant hermaphrodites were also immune to brief mating.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Day 7 (sperm-exhausted) raga-1 mutant hermaphrodites were immune to brief mating.
source: Similarly, RNAi reduction of other TOR pathway components, including rict-1, daf-15, and raga-1, also prevented brief mating-induced death in Day 3 fog-2 females, and Day 7 (sperm-exhausted) raga-1 mutant hermaphrodites were also immune to brief mating.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 5F.

claim: Downregulation of the TOR pathway is protective against mating-induced death.
source: Together, these results suggest that downregulation of the TOR pathway is protective (Figure 5E–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is an inference from the effects of TOR pathway component reduction.

claim: hlh-30(tm1978);let-363(RNAi) animals died faster after brief mating.
source: To test whether TOR's effects are mediated by HLH-30, we subjected hlh-30(tm1978);let-363(RNAi) animals to brief mating, and found that these animals died faster (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H), suggesting that HLH-30 acts downstream of TOR signaling to regulate brief mating-induced death.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 5G.

claim: HLH-30 acts downstream of TOR signaling to regulate brief mating-induced death.
source: To test whether TOR's effects are mediated by HLH-30, we subjected hlh-30(tm1978);let-363(RNAi) animals to brief mating, and found that these animals died faster (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H), suggesting that HLH-30 acts downstream of TOR signaling to regulate brief mating-induced death.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic epistasis experiment.

claim: Reduction of TOR/let-363 prevents cytoplasmic localization of HLH-30 upon mating.
source: Furthermore, reduction of TOR/let-363 prevents cytoplasmic localization of HLH-30 upon mating (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C), consistent with its prevention of brief mating-induced killing (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 5H.

claim: TOR promotes SF-mediated killing through its inhibition of TFEB/HLH-30 nuclear localization and activation.
source: Together, these results suggest that TOR promotes SF-mediated killing through its inhibition of TFEB/HLH-30 nuclear localization and activation.
evidence: This is an inference from the TOR pathway experiments and HLH-30 localization data.

claim: PQM-1 acts downstream of IIS and antagonistically to DAF-16/FOXO nuclear localization under normal conditions.
source: Previously, we found that the Zn-finger transcription factor PQM-1 acts downstream of IIS and antagonistically to DAF-16/FOXO nuclear localization under normal conditions (Tepper et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: pqm-1 mutant males are immune to both mating-induced and male pheromone-induced death.
source: pqm-1 mutant males are immune to both mating-induced and male pheromone-induced death (Shi et al., 2017), but PQM-1's role in hermaphroditic death was unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: pqm-1 mutants are impervious to brief mating.
source: Unlike daf-16 mutants, which are susceptible to brief mating even as young adults (Figure 2A), pqm-1 mutants are impervious to brief mating (Figure 6A); in fact, they are even resistant to long-term (24 hr) mating (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 6A.

claim: pqm-1 mutants are resistant to long-term (24 hr) mating.
source: Unlike daf-16 mutants, which are susceptible to brief mating even as young adults (Figure 2A), pqm-1 mutants are impervious to brief mating (Figure 6A); in fact, they are even resistant to long-term (24 hr) mating (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 6B.

claim: PQM-1 translocates into the nucleus upon mating.
source: While DAF-16 leaves the nucleus upon mating (Shi and Murphy, 2014) (Figure 2C–D), PQM-1 translocates into the nucleus (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 6C-E.

claim: PQM-1 activity is key for seminal fluid-induced killing.
source: These results suggest that PQM-1 activity is key for seminal fluid-induced killing, acting in an opposite manner to DAF-16/FOXO.
evidence: This is an inference from the pqm-1 mutant phenotype and localization data.

claim: PQM-1 acts in an opposite manner to DAF-16/FOXO.
source: These results suggest that PQM-1 activity is key for seminal fluid-induced killing, acting in an opposite manner to DAF-16/FOXO.
evidence: This is an inference from the contrasting phenotypes and localization patterns of pqm-1 and daf-16 mutants.

claim: pqm-1(RNAi) has no effect on the localization of HLH-30::GFP in unmated day 3 adult worms.
source: pqm-1(RNAi) appears to have no effect on the localization of HLH-30::GFP in unmated day 3 adult worms (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Reduction of pqm-1 prevented HLH-30 translocation out of the nucleus under mated conditions.
source: By contrast, under mated conditions (where HLH-30 normally traffics out of the nucleus, 'control mated' in Figure 6F), reduction of pqm-1 prevented this translocation (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 6F.

claim: Reduction of pqm-1 prevented the mating-induced lifespan decrease exhibited by hlh-30 reduction.
source: Consistent with a role in the regulation of HLH-30 localization after mating, reduction of pqm-1 also prevented the mating-induced lifespan decrease exhibited by hlh-30 reduction (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 6G.

claim: PQM-1 normally acts downstream of the seminal fluid/IIS pathway and antagonistically to HLH-30.
source: Together, these results suggest that PQM-1 normally acts downstream of the seminal fluid/IIS pathway and antagonistically to HLH-30, and that PQM-1 activity is deleterious to the mother when induced upon the transfer of seminal fluid upon mating.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic and localization experiments.

claim: PQM-1 activity is deleterious to the mother when induced upon the transfer of seminal fluid upon mating.
source: Together, these results suggest that PQM-1 normally acts downstream of the seminal fluid/IIS pathway and antagonistically to HLH-30, and that PQM-1 activity is deleterious to the mother when induced upon the transfer of seminal fluid upon mating.
evidence: This is an inference from the pqm-1 mutant resistance to mating-induced death.

claim: Upon mating, fog-2 hermaphrodites express strikingly higher levels of ins-8 than do pqm-1 hermaphrodites.
source: Indeed, upon mating, fog-2 hermaphrodites (which are killed by brief mating) express strikingly higher levels of ins-8 than do pqm-1 hermaphrodites, which are not affected by brief mating (Figure 7A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data in Figure 7A.

claim: Mating significantly increased the expression level of ins-8p::gfp, particularly in the anterior part of the intestine.
source: We confirmed the transcriptome analysis using a transcriptional reporter: mating significantly increased the expression level of ins-8p::gfp, particularly in the anterior part of the intestine (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by reporter imaging data in Figure 7B.

claim: INS-7 has been previously shown to act as a DAF-2 agonist that shortens lifespan.
source: INS-7, which has been previously shown to act as a DAF-2 agonist that shortens lifespan (Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2007), and functions in a feed-forward loop to reduce DAF-2 activity (Murphy et al., 2007), is also consistently induced but to a lesser degree.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: INS-7 functions in a feed-forward loop to reduce DAF-2 activity.
source: INS-7, which has been previously shown to act as a DAF-2 agonist that shortens lifespan (Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2007), and functions in a feed-forward loop to reduce DAF-2 activity (Murphy et al., 2007), is also consistently induced but to a lesser degree.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Knockdown of ins-8 blocked the lifespan-shortening effect of brief mating in fog-2 females.
source: Indeed, while brief mating of Day three fog-2 females with wild-type males shortens lifespan (Figure 7E), knockdown of ins-8 (Figure 7C) or ins-7 (Figure 7D) blocked this effect.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 7C.

claim: Knockdown of ins-7 blocked the lifespan-shortening effect of brief mating in fog-2 females.
source: Indeed, while brief mating of Day three fog-2 females with wild-type males shortens lifespan (Figure 7E), knockdown of ins-8 (Figure 7C) or ins-7 (Figure 7D) blocked this effect.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 7D.

claim: Reduction of ins-7 and ins-8 prevented HLH-30 cytoplasmic localization after mating.
source: Similar to loss of pqm-1 and TOR/let-363, reduction of ins-7 and ins-8 prevented HLH-30 cytoplasmic localization after mating (Figure 7F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 7F.

claim: INS-8 and INS-7 activity promote seminal fluid-induced killing.
source: Thus, INS-8 and INS-7 activity promote seminal fluid-induced killing and, like PQM-1 and TOR, act upstream of HLH-30.
evidence: This is an inference from the ins-7 and ins-8 knockdown phenotypes.

claim: INS-8 and INS-7 act upstream of HLH-30.
source: Thus, INS-8 and INS-7 activity promote seminal fluid-induced killing and, like PQM-1 and TOR, act upstream of HLH-30.
evidence: This is an inference from the effects of ins-7 and ins-8 knockdown on HLH-30 localization.

claim: The presence of self-sperm in hermaphroditic mothers slows the deleterious effects of mating with males.
source: The presence of self-sperm in hermaphroditic mothers slows the deleterious effects of mating with males, whose seminal fluid pathway 'hijacks' the mother's longevity and stress protection system by altering the activity of three important transcription factors, DAF-16 (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and as we show here, PQM-1 and HLH-30.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Male seminal fluid pathway 'hijacks' the mother's longevity and stress protection system by altering the activity of DAF-16, PQM-1 and HLH-30.
source: The presence of self-sperm in hermaphroditic mothers slows the deleterious effects of mating with males, whose seminal fluid pathway 'hijacks' the mother's longevity and stress protection system by altering the activity of three important transcription factors, DAF-16 (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and as we show here, PQM-1 and HLH-30.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of self-sperm staves off mating effects by inducing the expression of the insulin receptor antagonist, INS-37.
source: The presence of self-sperm staves off mating effects by inducing the expression of the insulin receptor antagonist, INS-37, which in turn prevents DAF-2/insulin signaling and retains DAF-16 and HLH-30 in the nucleus, and PQM-1 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: INS-37 prevents DAF-2/insulin signaling and retains DAF-16 and HLH-30 in the nucleus, and PQM-1 in the cytoplasm.
source: The presence of self-sperm staves off mating effects by inducing the expression of the insulin receptor antagonist, INS-37, which in turn prevents DAF-2/insulin signaling and retains DAF-16 and HLH-30 in the nucleus, and PQM-1 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: INS-8 and INS-7 expression is upregulated in mated mothers.
source: INS-8 and INS-7 expression is upregulated in mated mothers and inducing seminal-fluid-mediated killing through activation of DAF-2 and subsequent inhibition of DAF-16 (Shi and Murphy, 2014; Lin et al., 2001) and HLH-30 nuclear localization and activation.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome and reporter data.

claim: INS-8 and INS-7 induce seminal-fluid-mediated killing through activation of DAF-2 and subsequent inhibition of DAF-16 and HLH-30 nuclear localization and activation.
source: INS-8 and INS-7 expression is upregulated in mated mothers and inducing seminal-fluid-mediated killing through activation of DAF-2 and subsequent inhibition of DAF-16 (Shi and Murphy, 2014; Lin et al., 2001) and HLH-30 nuclear localization and activation.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and citations.

claim: INS-7 induction in the intestine and its feed-forward effect on DAF-2 coordinates the IIS pathway across the entire animal.
source: INS-7 induction in the intestine and its feed-forward effect on DAF-2 coordinates the IIS pathway across the entire animal (Murphy et al., 2007), which causes rapid deceleration of stress responsive pathways.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: INS-7's feed-forward effect causes rapid deceleration of stress responsive pathways.
source: INS-7 induction in the intestine and its feed-forward effect on DAF-2 coordinates the IIS pathway across the entire animal (Murphy et al., 2007), which causes rapid deceleration of stress responsive pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of INS-7 and the observed effects.

claim: PQM-1 drives HLH-30 out of the nucleus in an antagonistic manner, as PQM-1 does with DAF-16/FOXO.
source: PQM-1 appears to drive HLH-30 out of the nucleus in an antagonistic manner, as PQM-1 does with DAF-16/FOXO (Tepper et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: PQM-1 is negatively regulated by TOR signaling.
source: Like HLH-30, PQM-1 is negatively regulated by TOR signaling (Dowen et al., 2016), but since PQM-1's role is detrimental, the loss of each of these factors prevents mating-induced death (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The loss of PQM-1 prevents mating-induced death.
source: Like HLH-30, PQM-1 is negatively regulated by TOR signaling (Dowen et al., 2016), but since PQM-1's role is detrimental, the loss of each of these factors prevents mating-induced death (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data showing pqm-1 mutants are resistant to mating-induced death.

claim: The expression of a DAF-2 antagonist, INS-37, allows hermaphrodites to resist and delay seminal fluid-induced killing until self-sperm are exhausted.
source: The expression of a DAF-2 antagonist, INS-37, allows hermaphrodites to resist and delay C. elegans' main mechanism of competition with other males, seminal fluid-induced killing, until self-sperm are exhausted, increasing the chances that the mother will survive through the end of her reproductive period.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: INS-37 increases the chances that the mother will survive through the end of her reproductive period.
source: The expression of a DAF-2 antagonist, INS-37, allows hermaphrodites to resist and delay C. elegans' main mechanism of competition with other males, seminal fluid-induced killing, until self-sperm are exhausted, increasing the chances that the mother will survive through the end of her reproductive period.
evidence: This is an inference from the protective role of INS-37 and self-sperm.

claim: Increased attraction of males accompanies the depletion of self-sperm.
source: Such strategies, coupled with the increased attraction of males that accompany the depletion of self-sperm (Morsci et al., 2011), enable hermaphrodites to delay both the odds of mating, through behavioral changes (Morsci et al., 2011) and the detrimental effects of mating (through molecular signaling), before the full utilization of their own sperm.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hermaphrodites delay both the odds of mating through behavioral changes and the detrimental effects of mating through molecular signaling before the full utilization of their own sperm.
source: Such strategies, coupled with the increased attraction of males that accompany the depletion of self-sperm (Morsci et al., 2011), enable hermaphrodites to delay both the odds of mating, through behavioral changes (Morsci et al., 2011) and the detrimental effects of mating (through molecular signaling), before the full utilization of their own sperm.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and citations.

claim: This insulin peptide-based arms race regulates a transition from preventing to promoting the activation of the insulin signaling pathway.
source: This insulin peptide-based arms race regulates a transition from preventing to promoting the activation of the insulin signaling pathway, resulting first in protection from death during early reproduction, and then accelerated death of the mother immediately after reproduction.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The insulin peptide-based arms race results first in protection from death during early reproduction, and then accelerated death of the mother immediately after reproduction.
source: This insulin peptide-based arms race regulates a transition from preventing to promoting the activation of the insulin signaling pathway, resulting first in protection from death during early reproduction, and then accelerated death of the mother immediately after reproduction.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
